Before the reading
Thursday, 18 October 2035, half past six in the evening. In half an hour Ludwig's reading begins in the café «Bei Ingrid». Ludwig has stage fright. Lena is trying to calm him down.
Lena, how many people are outside?
More than will fit in the café. The queue goes all the way to the corner.
That's bad. I wasn't expecting so many people.
“I wasn't expecting so many people” is how you say it, Grandpa. You're a writer now.
You see, I'm so nervous I can't even put my verbs in the right place any more.
Don't worry, Mr Brandt. Everyone does that in conversation. By the way, I've ordered more books than for any other reading this year. Two hundred.
Two hundred? And what if nobody buys a single one?
Then you'll have enough Christmas presents until the year two thousand and sixty.
You read for twenty minutes, after that there are questions, and at the end you sign the books for everyone who wants to buy one.
Which story shall I read first?
The first one. The one about the tram and the twelve books. You wrote it to read it today. Even if you didn't know it.
All right. Then give me my glasses. And don't tell anyone I wear glasses.

1. The sentence bracket

In German, the conjugated verb stands in position 2, and the rest of the verb (participle, infinitive, particle) goes to the end. Between them is the “bracket” (Satzklammer). Whatever comes after the second part of the verb is called the Nachfeld.

2. What usually goes in the Nachfeld
comparisons with als / wie
Das Café war voller als je zuvor.
subordinate clauses (dass, weil, ob…)
Er hat gesagt, dass er aufgeregt ist.
infinitives with zu, um … zu
Sie hat versucht, ihn zu beruhigen.
long relative clauses
Er signierte Bücher für alle, die gekommen waren.
A comparison with “als” almost always comes after the final verb: “Er hat mehr verkauft als erwartet”, not “Er hat mehr als erwartet verkauft” (possible, but clumsier).
3. Ausklammerung in speech

In conversation, Germans often move prepositional phrases after the verb too, so they don't have to hold too much in their heads: “Ich hab gewartet auf dich.” “Wir treffen uns morgen um acht vor dem Kino.” → “Wir treffen uns morgen vor dem Kino um acht.”
In writing, in an exam, put short prepositional phrases inside: “Ich habe mit so vielen Menschen nicht gerechnet”, as Lena corrected Ludwig.
4. Why it matters

A sentence with too much information between the two parts of the verb becomes hard to follow: “Er hat das Buch für alle Gäste, die aus ganz Deutschland, aus Wien und sogar aus Sibiu gekommen waren, signiert.” Clearer: “Er hat das Buch signiert für alle Gäste, die …” or, more standard: “Er hat das Buch für alle Gäste signiert, die …”
Rule of thumb: if the reader has to wait too long for the verb, move the long part (especially the subordinate clause) into the Nachfeld.
I wasn't expecting so many people.
He came to Berlin to study.
He read the way he always speaks: slowly.
She tried to calm him down.

Die Lesung

On Thursday, the eighteenth of October two thousand and thirty-five, the café «Bei Ingrid» was fuller than it had ever been, fuller than at the opening, fuller than at Mara's wedding, fuller even than on the evening when the square outside the door had been named after Ingrid. Lena had carried all the tables out into the courtyard and put chairs in their place instead, in rows, as in a theatre, eighty chairs, which she had borrowed from the parish hall, from the school and from the Yilmaz family. By half past six they were all taken. By a quarter to seven people were standing along the walls. By seven they were standing outside in the square, in front of the big windows through which you could see inside, and Andrei hastily set up a loudspeaker so that they could hear something too.

Who had come, nobody could say exactly afterwards, not even Katrin Krüger, who tried to make a list and gave up after sixty names. The family was there, of course: Sabine from Potsdam, who had taken time off from the library, and Thomas, who had come with Anja from Treptow and sat in the last row because, as he said, he didn't want to get in the way. Leo came straight from his evening shift, in his BVG uniform, and with him three colleagues from the depot, who didn't know Ludwig but had heard of him, because the photograph of his last run with the old Tatra had been hanging at BVG headquarters for years. Neighbours from Kastanienallee came, and people from all over Berlin who had read Katrin's article. Ingrid's former pupils came, grey-haired people who introduced themselves with their name and the year they had been in her class: “Nineteen seventy-eight, third row by the window.” And a group came from Mrs Krause's German course at the town hall, twelve people from nine countries, who wanted to read the book together, one story a week, for a whole year.

Ludwig saw none of this. He was sitting in the little kitchen behind the counter, on a stool, between the coffee machine and the sink, with his book on his knees, and he had stage fright, as he had last had it in nineteen sixty-eight, on his first day as a tram driver. Back then his instructor had given him a piece of advice that he remembered now: “Don't look at the people getting on. Look at the rails.” He opened the book, the first copy, which Mrs Winter had brought him two weeks before, and looked at the pages. At the rails. At the words he had written himself and which suddenly seemed strange to him, printed, orderly, in a typeface that wasn't his.

The book had turned out beautiful, more beautiful than he had imagined it. It was bound in dark green cloth, like the old books on Ingrid's shelf, and on the cover was the brass bell, photographed by Andrei, with the little sign beside it that said: “Klingeln erlaubt” (ringing allowed). Above it, in simple gold letters: “Ludwig Brandt. Geschichten der Kastanienallee.” On the first page was the dedication, which he had added only at the last moment, after thinking for three nights about what to write: “For Ingrid, who showed me that a book can be better than music. And for everyone who has rung the bell of this house.”

At five past seven Mrs Winter came into the kitchen, in a dark blue dress, with a glass of water in her hand. “It's time, Mr Brandt,” she said. “There are more people waiting out there than I've ever seen at a reading. And I've been doing this for twenty-seven years.” Ludwig stood up, slowly, took his stick and his book and followed her out, through the narrow door behind the counter, into the room, where suddenly there was complete silence. Eighty people on chairs and forty along the walls and as many again outside, behind the glass, all turned towards him at once. Ludwig stood still. Then he did what his instructor had advised. He didn't look at the people. He looked at the chair in the front row, where someone was sitting whom he hadn't expected.

It was Grete. She was sitting in a wheelchair, wrapped in a thick red blanket, with a hat on her head that Ludwig had never seen her wear, a little black hat with a feather, which looked as if it came from the fifties, and it did. Beside her sat Mara, who had brought her from the care home, against the doctor's advice but with the express permission of the patient herself, who, as Mara told later, had said: “I'm ninety-nine. If I don't go to a reading now, then when?” Grete raised her hand, just a little, and waved to him. Ludwig forgot his stage fright. He went to the table with the microphone, sat down, put on his glasses, without caring who saw, and began to read.

His voice trembled on the first sentence. On the second, already less. By the third he had forgotten that two hundred people were listening to him and was reading only for the woman with the little black hat in the front row, who had closed her eyes, as she always did when she listened to music.

He read the first story, the one about the tram and the twelve books, and he read it more slowly than he had ever read anything, the way he used to drive, without hurrying, with pauses in the right places. When he came to Hotte's sentences, which were in Berlin dialect in the book, he looked up, over his glasses, at the third row, where Hotte was sitting with his tram driver's cap on his knees, and he read them the way Hotte had said them, with the broad “ick” and the soft “j”, and the whole room laughed, and Hotte called out loudly: “That's exactly how it was!” And when Ludwig came to the place where the young woman stepped out from behind the books and he recognised her, his voice grew quieter, and the room was so silent that you could hear the tram ringing outside in the square.

Then came the questions. A student wanted to know whether all the stories were true. “All of them,” said Ludwig. “Although some are truer than others. In one it snowed first, even though it had been raining. The editor found that. And an eleven-year-old editor.” Elif, who was sitting in the second row, blushed. An older gentleman asked whether Ludwig would still drive the tram if he could. “Every day,” said Ludwig. “But they won't let me. I'm too slow for the timetable.” Then a boy of about ten put his hand up, who was standing right at the back by the wall, and asked whether you can write a book when you're not good at German. Ludwig looked at him for a long time. “You know,” he said, “I wrote the first sentence of this book at eighty-six. Before that I just listened, for sixty years. It starts with listening. The writing comes by itself.”

The last question came from the last row. Thomas had stood up, and Ludwig only saw him when he spoke. “I have a question for the author,” said Thomas, and his voice was firmer than Ludwig remembered it. “Which story am I in?” There was silence. Many people in the room knew the old story between father and son, the years when they hadn't spoken. Ludwig took off his glasses. “None of them,” he said. “And all of them. You're the reason I started to listen. Too late, but not too late.” Thomas sat back down. Sabine, who was sitting next to him, took his hand, and neither of them said anything more until the end of the reading.

At the end he signed books. He signed for two hours, for everyone who had bought one, and more people had bought one than Mrs Winter had ordered. The two hundred copies were sold out by half past eight, and Mrs Winter, her eyes shining, rang her printers to order a second print run that very evening, even though nobody was answering the phone there any more. For those who hadn't got a book, Ludwig signed napkins, receipts and, in one case, the plaster cast on the arm of a little girl from the primary school. Michael Kühn came with an old, well-thumbed copy of “Emil und die Detektive” (Emil and the Detectives), the very one Ingrid had taught him to read from almost forty years earlier, and asked Ludwig to sign it. “It's not my book,” said Ludwig. “Yes, it is,” said Michael. “Now it is.”

Right at the end, when most people had left, Mara pushed Grete's wheelchair to the table. Grete hadn't bought a book. She had brought something else: a small, yellowed programme from the Konzerthaus, from nineteen fifty-six, from her first concert, which said in tiny letters: “At the piano: Margarete Hoffmann, aged 20.” “Sign here,” she whispered, pointing to the empty margin beside her name. “So that we're there together. The pianist and the writer.” Ludwig took the pen. His hand was shaking, more than usual. He wrote, slowly, in his large, slightly crooked handwriting: “For Grete, who played first. From Ludwig, who wrote last.” Grete read it, nodded contentedly and put the programme in her handbag. “This one,” she said, “I'm taking with me.” Nobody asked where.

When Mara had left with Grete, and Lena was stacking the chairs and Andrei was taking down the loudspeaker, Ludwig stayed at the table a while longer, alone, with the last copy of his book, which Mrs Winter had put aside for him. Outside in the square it had grown dark. The street lamp in front of the “Ingrid-Brandt-Platz” sign was lit. Ludwig opened the book at the page with the dedication and read it once more. Then he took the pen and wrote underneath, small, in the empty corner, a sentence that nobody but him would ever read, because this was the copy he wanted to put on Ingrid's old shelf, on the far right, next to “Emil und die Detektive”. The sentence went: “I did it, Ingrid. With commas.”
